#3205. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3204. The Best Tech Deals From Walmart’s 2026 Black Friday Sale

The second of Walmart's three major sales for Black Friday and Cyber Monday is now live, and there are some amazing tech deals to take advantage of. I've gathered my top 10 tech products from the sale below. For more, keep tabs on our Black Friday coverage, where we post the latest deals from not just Walmart, but Amazon, Best Buy, and other retailers' Black Friday sales.

Apple's latest smartwatch is the Series 12, but don't count out the Series 11. By sacrificing a few of Apple's newest features, you can save some money on the more premium version of this last-gen Apple Watch. Right now, the Titanium Series 11 GPS + cellular model is on sale for $489.30 (originally $699).

During WWDC 26 earlier this summer, Apple announced new Siri AI upgrades with watchOS 27—but only some Apple Watches have compatibility. Luckily, the Series 11 is one of them, at least for many of them. Some other upgrades in the new OS include a dedicated Siri app, a new app grid, a new single-tap gesture, among other features. Just note that only Series 12 and Ultra 4 can run Audio Intelligence.

The Garmin vivoactive 5 was $299.99 when it first came out in 2023 as their midrange lifestyle-focused fitness smartwatch. It features a 1.2-inch AMOLED touchscreen and an 11-day battery life (four to five days with the always-on display setting). You can get it for $169.99 right now. It's a great option for anyone looking to get into Garmin for the first time or upgrading from anything below it.

Bone conduction headphones are ideal for activities where it is vital to be able to hear your surroundings. They use a technology that sends audio vibrations to your inner ear while leaving your ear canals open. Shokz is one of, if not the best, brands making bone conduction headphones right now. At the high end of Shokz's offerings sit the OpenRun Pro 2, which impressed me when I tested them out for review. Walmart currently has a restored pair for $93 (originally $179.99 new).

The latest AirPods Pro are a big step up. The third iteration of Apple's iconic earbuds comes with a number of quality-of-life and software improvements that make them worth the typical premium over the AirPods Pro 2—and right now, the AirPods Pro 3 are even cheaper than the previous generation. They're $149 on Walmart as an Black Friday deal, down from $249 and matching their lowest price ever.

Most, if not all, TV speakers aren't great. While you have plenty of options, the quickest and least expensive way to improve your TV's audio capabilities is to buy a soundbar. Compare a soundbar's size to the thin, small speakers jammed into modern TVs. The Vizio 5.1 Pro Soundbar with a subwoofer and rear speakers supports Dolby Atmos and costs just $99 (originally $198). They won't win any audio awards, but it's better than any built-in TV speakers, and for $99, it'll improve your experience without breaking the bank.

If you want to take things up a notch, consider this 5.1 channel sound system. While it's a 5.1 system as well, it reaches a 312W peak power, which will make explosions and thuds feel more realistic. There's also a dedicated dialogue feature for people who don't like using subtitles. For $149.99 (originally $249.99), you can get the ULTIMEA 5.1 surround sound system.

I love projectors and Roku. To me, a Roku projector just makes sense, especially at $119.99 (originally $389.99). This projector is portable and has the Roku OS already installed, so it's easy to project it against a wall, ceiling, or screen, whether it's indoors or outdoors. It's easy to set up; you just need an outlet nearby and to dim or turn off the lights. If you have Bluetooth speakers, you can hook them up to create a more immersive sound.

The TCL Q51GB is a QLED Google TV that is a great value for anyone looking for size, color, and features. The 98-inch class is heavily discounted at its $898 price (originally $1,499.99). TCL makes one of the best QLEDs for the money, and their technology keeps getting better. This TV supports Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, and if you're a gamer, you get a refresh rate of 240Hz that is automatically triggered with its Auto Game Mode feature.

If you've been holding off on buying a Nintendo Switch 2 until it went on sale and better games were available, now might be the time to pull the trigger. Right now, Walmart is offering the Mario World bundle for $499 (originally $549). The timing of this deal is even more noteworthy, given that Nintendo recently released the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

Gaming monitors can get pricey fast. At $159.99 (originally $299.99 at launch), this 27-inch Samsung Odyssey G55C curved gaming monitor offers a 1440p resolution, a 1000R curve, a 165Hz refresh rate with FreeSync and G-SYNC compatibility to keep screen tearing to a minimum, and features like Samsung’s Virtual Aim Point and Contrast Enhancer. It's a solid choice for gaming, especially at this price point.

Alienware makes great gaming laptops, and the Aurora is a great option for anyone who wants to get all the essentials without spending too much. At its current $1,099 price (originally $1,999), the Alienware Aurora 16 becomes a mid-tier gaming laptop at a "budget" price. We reviewed the higher-tier Aurora 16X and were impressed with it. The Aurora 16 has a slightly slower processor, a dimmer display with half the refresh rate, a smaller battery, and a weaker graphics card, but given its price, it's great for a gamer looking for a solid gaming laptop in the $1,000 range.

Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Amazon has a much larger inventory of tech products on sale, but the ones they both sell are mostly priced the same. While Amazon may have more deals, Walmart usually has a couple of surprise flagship tech products on sale that Amazon will later price match. So taking all of that into consideration, the best one will be whichever has whatever you're looking to buy at the lower price.

EXCLUSIVE: Former NBA champion and All-Star David M. West is stepping into the world of filmmaking as screenwriter and executive producer of The Neighbor, a psychological thriller inspired by true events and directed by Kyle Scott.

Principal photography began November 4, 2026, in Cape Town, South Africa, where production is currently underway.

Head to the Festivitas website to get started and bring some holiday cheer to your Apple devices.

It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single TV in need of decent sound must be in want of one of the best soundbars. And, likely, you're here because you're sick of awful-sounding TV speakers — well, I've got the list for you. We've spent a lot of time testing the best soundbars to make sure you get the best bang for your buck.

The best is still the Sonos Arc Ultra. It's an absolute stunner of a soundbar, bringing great sound, lovely Dolby Atmos, and even slick styling so you won't mind it sitting under your TV. It does come with a big wallet-denting price, though — if you're looking to save some money, we'd go for the also excellent Sony HT-S100F.

But each soundbar we've listed here would make a great addition to your TV setup, so whether you're shopping on a budget, need something to work with your existing tech or just need a few more options to choose from, these are the best soundbars we've tested that I recommend right now.

The Tom's Guide testing team is an experienced bunch who love good sound. Here's why you can trust us to find the best soundbar for your needs:

From the time I built a surround system from the cheapest stuff I could find on eBay to reviewing the latest and greatest sound gear, I put a whole lot of time and effort into working out which soundbars are worth your money. I've constructed this guide with input from the rest of the team so that we can use our experience to guide you through your soundbar journey.

When I’m testing soundbars, I put them through their paces in our state-of-the-art testing suite, complete with a top-of-the-range Panasonic OLED TV and an array of 4K Ultra HD Blu-Rays. I’m looking for soundbars that make movies come to life — both budget-friendly and premium.

As a reviews writer, I put soundbars through rigorous testing by analyzing sound quality across various film and TV genres, connectivity options, and determine whether they're the best value for money. I love watching movies at the theater, so I like a soundbar that can closely replicate the sound via Dolby Atmos. I also play a lot of video games on my PS5 and there's nothing better than a soundbar that makes you feel like you're actually a sword-wielding samurai in feudal Japan.

Before we dive deep into the best soundbars, I just want to go through what we look for when we're testing them. We make sure to evaluate the soundbar in some key areas.

Setup: While it's something you're only going to do once, we want to make sure that it's as easy as possible to get working. Plug-and-play is the name of the game here, and if there are extra features we want to make sure that they're as easy as possible to use.

How big is it? Everyone's space is different. Maybe you've got a massive room with loads of stuff in it, or maybe your living room is more compact and minimal. You want a soundbar that's going to suit your space, and, more importantly, not going to take up too much of it. We check whether the soundbar fits under our 50-inch OLED Philips testing TV to make sure you're not going to have any size issues. Ultimately, it needs to fit on your TV stand.

Are there any extras? What's in the box, and are its contents any good? Some soundbars come with extras like surround speakers and subwoofers. I want to make sure that those extras are worth it, and that they're not just pictures to sell them at the store.

Sound: This is arguably the most important part of the soundbar, and there are a number of things we look out for here. How's the dialog? Is it clear, or muffled? What about the bass — are you going to have rumbling floors in your movies, or are there going to be problems with the low end? I love testing the sound portion because I get to watch movies instead of working; But it's still important when testing and working out whether a bar is for you.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Sonos Arc Ultra is the best soundbar around. It's not cheap, but it's surround sound and Dolby Atmos performance beats just about anything else that lacks separate surround speakers. I'll almost certainly never watch movies with anything else for some time.

The Sonos Arc Ultra is more than just a soundbar. It's a fully fledged audio entertainment center that connects to your TV and just happens to be really good for movies and TV.

I particularly like how you can stream your music to it from any device — I frequently find myself spending a bunch of time listening to my favorite tunes from Qobuz and Tidal with it, thanks to its ease of use.

But it's really that epic movie experience you're looking for with something like the Sonos Arc Ultra, and you get it in spades. The Dolby Atmos with just the soundbar is unlike anything else around, and if you add in the optional surrounds, it's a game-changer.

I absolutely love watching just about anything with the Arc Ultra — although you will want to pick up a Sonos sub so that you can get the low-end grunt your movies deserve. It's not cheap — but it is so, so worth it.

SetupSetting up your Arc Ultra is going to take a bit more effort than some of the other options on the list. I found it fairly easy though, given the excellent instructions. If all you want to do is use the soundbar, you just plug it into power, plug the HDMI port into the back of the soundbar and the HDMI ARC port of your TV, and it should work without problems at all. I did have to change the settings in my Samsung TV sound menu to make sure that the device was set as the primary sound output, but then it worked with no problem.

If you want to use the excellent Sonos room correction settings, smart features, or to connect other Sonos speakers as surrounds, things will get more complicated. You'll need to use the Sonos App for these — and while it's not difficult, it is extra work. The room correction options also need you to move around the room while waving your phone around, so if mobility is something you struggle with, you may want to look elsewhere.

Once set up, you won't have any issues, but it's worth bearing in mind that it takes more work to get it working. It's all absolutely worth your time though, with massive boosts to sound quality and useful features within the Sonos App.

How big is itThe Sonos Arc Ultra is a big soundbar. It's very long, measuring around four feet long. I found it perfectly suited for TVs larger than 55 inches, although if your TV is smaller, things might look out of place.

There's less of a problem with the height. It's only about 3 inches tall, so it'll fit under most TVs without a problem.

Are there any extrasYou get the soundbar in a box — there's no included subwoofer here. Not that you really need one, though, given that Sonos has managed to pack some incredible bassy hardware into its slim frame.

If you want to enhance your movie-watching experience, though, you can add in a Sonos sub and surrounds in the form of Era 100 or Era 300 speakers. It adds to the cost, but it gets very close to dedicated home cinema sound.

SoundThis is the best bit of the Arc Ultra. I love the way that soundbar sounds for movies and TV, with some incredible body to the sound. I found the dialogue clear while watching the news and other TV shows, and it was excellent when listening to Sir David Attenborough talk to me about dinosaurs in Prehistoric Planet.

For movies, as you might expect, the Arc Ultra dominates. I discovered that even without extra surrounds, the Dolby Atmos was amazing, putting me in the center of a space battle in Star Wars Episode 3. The bass without a sub is surprisingly good as well, although if you really want to feel your movies you should buy the extra subwoofer.

It's pretty good for music as well, uncommon for a soundbar. There's plenty of space, thanks to the wider form factor, and the bar manages the low end of your tracks pretty well, too.

The Sony HT-S100F (HT-S150 in the U.K.) is a great-sounding soundbar for an epic price. It won't break the bank, but it'll increase the sound quality of your movies and TV far and above the sound from your TV speakers.

When you don't want to spend loads of money on a soundbar, something like the Sony HT-S100F is just what the doctor ordered. It's a lovely, cheap soundbar that does everything you need it to — make your TV sound better than the built-in audio.

It brings more clarity to dialogue, most importantly. Everything from your favorite movies all the way to news bulletins and everything in between become much easier to make out, perfect if you're struggling to hear what people are trying to say.

It's relatively compact as well, so you'll have no problems fitting it on your TV bench beneath most sizes of screen. Our tester found it super easy to use, with very few (if any) connection issues that sometimes plague cheaper devices.

It's not going to be as impressive as some of the more expensive options on the list, but it more than makes up for it with excellent clarity for all your watching.

SetupGetting the HT-S100F up and running is about as easy as they come. Just plug the power in, connect the HDMI port to the HDMI ARC on your TV, and it'll turn on automatically whenever you turn on your TV.

Erin did find that you might have to occasionally turn the bar on with the remote control, but it didn't happen enough to be a massive problem.

How big is itThe HT-S100F is designed for normal-sized televisions, and its compact frame will fit on most TV stands. It measures 35 inches long, so you'll be fine for TVs from 32 inches to 50.

It might seem a little small for larger TVs, though, with the screen dwarfing the soundbar beneath. You'll also find some minor sound issues with larger sets, as the picture feels wider than the sound that's coming out.

Height-wise you'll be fine with a range of different TVs as well. The bar measures just 2.5 inches tall, so it won't cover the bottom of your screen. If it covers the IR receiver of your TV, there's an IR repeater built in so that your controller still works.

Erin found it fit well underneath our 50-inch testing TV, although if you've got a larger TV set, you might want something slightly larger in the long run.

Are there any extras?In the box of the HT-S100F, you get the soundbar — and nothing else. You can't buy an extra subwoofer or surround either, leaving you with no upgrades for the future.

This makes it great for just a simple setup, and it keeps the cost down. There's a controller in the box as well, so you can connect Bluetooth devices and change sources without standing up.

SoundThe HT-100F isn't going to blow you away if you're a movie lover, but its solid, serviceable sound is a big step-up over your TV's built-in speakers. It makes dialog clearer, music sounds better, and sound effects are easier to hear.

For music, things weren't quite so impressive, but if you've got no other ways to listen to music in the living room, it will more than suffice. If you're looking for a cheap way to get much better sound out of your TV watching, then this is the way to go.

Sony's mid-range soundbar brings smarts and excellent sound to a more affordable price point. It connects to your Wi-Fi for wireless listening and includes a good subwoofer for some extra sonic grunt. It's excellent for dialogue too, with crystal-clear voice work for movies and TV shows alike.

Sony's line of soundbars can cost a lot of money — but it's the mid-range and cheap offerings that we recommend the most. This, the Theater Bar 7, is the mid-range bar, and it offers some great value for money.

For one, the 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos sound is very good. The included sub offers some extra low-end for those all-important explosions in action movies, and the surround sound is immersive and well produced. The dialogue department is where the soundbar really shines. Speech is clear and easily discernible over whatever else is going on on-screen.

There are also some useful smart features built in. You can connect to your Wi-Fi to stream music to the bar, and adjust settings from the app on your phone. As long as you don't expect the best musical sound, of course — as with so many soundbars, this is not a musical powerhouse but a rectangular movie hero. And that's OK.

Those with bigger TVs might also struggle slightly with the size. It's quite a compact soundbar, and that can affect the perception of sound in space when the image above it is much larger. Thankfully, the solid surround sound does a good job of keeping the effect to a minimum.

It should be noted that the Theater Bar 7 is not a cheap soundbar, but it's a great way of getting immersive sound without spending thousands on one of the range-topping devices.

SetupFor any normal movie or TV watching, setting up the bar is very easy. Plug it into the power, and then into the HDMI ARC port on your TV. Plug in the subwoofer and everything connects together with no hassle at all.

Nor is connecting the bar to the internet. Download the app, and then follow the on-screen instructions to get everything working properly. We recommend you dip into the settings menu from there and turn the bass up, and raise the surround height to 10. That gave us the best sound, although your room might require some fine tweaking.

How big is itThis is a fairly compact soundbar, measuring 37.5 inches long. That means that it's going to be dwarfed by larger TVs, but those measuring around 55 inches or smaller are going to be fine. Our testing TV is 55 inches, for example, and everything was fine.

The subwoofer is thin and compact too, so you don't need as much space as you might for some of the competition. It fits perfectly beside a TV unit without sticking out like a sore thumb.

Are there any extrasThere's one very big extra in the box beside the remote control — that lovely big subwoofer for the low stuff. There aren't any extra surround speakers though, because they're all built into the bar itself.

Features-wise, though, you've got the mobile app to go with Bluetooth and wired audio connections. You can stream music to the bar from around the house, should you want some music when you're not watching movies. You can also use the app to change key settings of the bar, like sound profiles and bass levels.

SoundSony's audio chops are well documented, and the Theater Bar 7 just continues the legacy. There's some lovely bass on offer here, with impact and depth whenever the action on screen gets thick and fast. We used the app to dial in the bass a bit, though; out of the box it was tuned a bit low. Your mileage may vary, of course.

The dialogue was what really impressed here, though. Speech was clear and bright no matter what was going on around it, be that a fighter plane screeching through the skies or a car chase in the Batmobile. That's not to say it's ever in your face. When the goings get calmer, the voices adjust to match. You'll never miss a word.

Not everything is rosy, as it generally isn't with most soundbars. Music playback is disappointing, with merely an "OK" in our review. It's not bad, but there's no drive to the music as you'll find with movies and TV shows. A shame, but not unexpected.

If you want a true surround sound package in one unit, then the 1300XMK2 could be just what you've been looking for. Its extra speakers attach to the bar itself, and then you can move them into position when you want to watch a movie. It's not cheap, but it's a movie monster.

There’s not really such a thing as a “bargain” when it comes to home surround sound. Instead, there’s value — and the JBL Bar 1300XMK2 brings the value unlike just about anything. Flexibility, a more affordable price than the key competition, and, of course, great sound.

The two ends of the soundbar can be disconnected and placed around the room, powered by their own internal batteries. If you don’t have the space for a traditional setup, this is a great way to enjoy immersive Dolby Atmos sound without a more permanent (and expensive) solution.

The soundbar itself is quite large, however. It’s very deep and rather long with its surrounds attached, so you’ll need a long TV stand and big TV to make sure it doesn’t look out of place. There’s a subwoofer in the box that you’ll need to find space for as well.

The sound is great. It’s immersive, directional, deep and clear. We loved it when watching a wide range of movies, from action to romance. There’s little this soundbar can’t do.

SetupFirst off, hit the gym before you place this soundbar anywhere. This is a 26-pound behemoth, so you might even want two people to lift it into place on your TV stand. There are some extra setup quirks as well, but they’re easily mitigated thanks to the good instructions and user-friendly design.

Once you’ve plugged the soundbar and subwoofer into the wall, you’ll hook the soundbar into the eARC port of your TV. The soundbar and sub should find each other automatically, but if not, use the connection button on the sub.

If you want to use the surrounds, pull them off the soundbar and place them around your room. Sound adjustment is done automatically. If you have any wireless connection issues, re-attach them to the soundbar to reset everything.

Streaming and Wi-Fi are handled by JBL’s ONE app. It’s super easy; we had no problems at all getting everything connected and working.

How big is itThere’s no two ways around it — the 1300XMK2 is a very big soundbar. At 40 inches, the soundbar is wide, and that's without taking extra surrounds into account. It’s very deep too, so you’ll want to make sure that there’s enough space on your TV stand that way. If not, we’d recommend wall mounting the TV.

This is a bar suited to much larger TVs, 65-inch at a minimum. Otherwise you’ll risk the bar looking too big, and your TV small.

Thankfully, you won’t have to worry about how tall the bar is. It’s short enough that most TVs will amply clear the top, so you don’t have to worry about the soundbar blocking the view. Just bear in mind that you’ll also want space for the surround speakers behind your seating position — they’re not going to work if they’re in front of you.

Are there any extrasYou get everything you need in the box. There’s the bar itself, along with the surround speakers. Unlike other models, from the likes of Sonos, this is a big bonus and means you don’t have to buy any further devices for some lovely Dolby Atmos sound.

There’s also a subwoofer in the box, along with all the cables you’d ever need for just about any circumstance. There’s a controller in the box, although we found that the JBL ONE app was a perfectly serviceable way of controlling the sound — or your TV remote through the eARC port.

SoundWith 23 drivers powering 11.1.4 channels, you’d hope the 1300XMK2 sounded good. And, sure enough, the bar sounds excellent. Those extra surrounds make sure that the sound is immersive and massive, while the sub adds impressive depth and bass.

The planes flying in Top Gun: Maverick made the room shake, and the soundtrack was bombastic during testing. The whole movie placed our tester directly in the movie.

Object placement is good too, making sure that everything is kept in the right place.

The soundbar was pretty good for music too, making soundtracks sound great, although it struggled slightly more with stereo tracks — but it's still better than most soundbars.

Want everything in one box but don't want to spend every single dollar you have? The QS750F is a great option, with extra surround speakers and a subwoofer for less than $1000.

Soundbars are expensive — there’s no way around that. You want to achieve the best bang-for-buck sound, right? Enter the Samsung QS750F. For a relatively low MSRP of $899, the QS750F gives you a soundbar, two rears, and a subwoofer, which is considerably more generous than Sonos or JBL.

As a result, the QS750F blows the competition out of the park. For under $1k, you get cinematic sound, with enviable width and immense bass. The QS750F sounds so good that we forgot we were supposed to be reviewing it.

Although it’s just a 5.1.2 channel configuration — considerably fewer speakers than JBL’s monstrous 1300XMK2, which boasts 11.1.4 channels and costs almost double — you probably wouldn’t be able to notice the difference.

SetupAs with every other soundbar, setup is a relatively quick process. Once the soundbar, subwoofer, and rears are unpackaged, simply connect everything to power and plug the soundbar into your TV using HDMI eARC.

Unlike JBL’s collection of premium soundbars, the QS750F’s rears aren’t truly “wireless” — sure, they connect to the soundbar wirelessly, but the left speaker must be connected to power. This is only an issue if you’re short on power outlets, extension cables, or if you want a particularly cable-free setup. Even so, you’re not going to get a better multi-speaker setup for less, so we think this is a worthy sacrifice.

The subwoofer is wireless, so don’t worry about needing to connect that to the soundbar with a wire. It’ll automatically connect.

How big is itAs you might expect, the QS750F is a large soundbar. This is true of pretty much every high-power soundbar — they’re designed to be able to fill large rooms with both size and physical presence.

The soundbar is 46 inches long and ten inches deep, so you’ll need to ensure it fits on your TV stand/wall mount and that your TV is big enough. I’d recommend anything from 55 inches up.

The subwoofer is effectively a 10 x 10 x 10-inch cube. We’d recommend positioning the subwoofer around 12 inches from the walls on all sides. You’ll need to play around with spacing to figure out the optimal position. Some setups come with configuration modes in the relevant app, but Samsung locks its proprietary Space Fit Pro behind post-2021 AI-powered Samsung TVs.

Are there any extrasThe QS750F comes with everything you need for a Dolby Atmos all-in-one setup. You get the soundbar, subwoofer, and two rears.

You also get AirPlay, Google Cast, and smart home features in the SmartThings app, which we’d recommend downloading. You can easily adjust playback modes and listening styles — movie, music, gaming, voice enhancement — to find what pleases you.

SoundAlright, now onto the most important part of any soundbar: its audio output. Thankfully, you’ll be pleased to know that the QS750F sounds utterly fantastic.

As the QS750F is a large soundbar, it’s intended for use in a large room. The side-firing speakers in the soundbar itself and the powerful subwoofer work together to create a wide soundscape worthy of a movie theater. Although there’s not as much height as width, the soundbar’s Dolby Atmos performance is still admirable.

The dialogue performance is a clear standout, though: I was never left wondering what was being said thanks to voice enhancement mode. This feature isolated dialogue well, and ensured even the moodiest and broodiest speech was crystal clear.

Most audiophiles will be the first to admit that soundbars aren’t ideal for playing music — me included — but the QS750F didn’t balk at the challenge. Although I’d much rather listen to music via my bookshelf speakers or headphones, the QS750F played every song with rich, pulsing bass, and would be good enough for a quick listening session or party.

Sonos' compact soundbar brings excellent sound with a slightly higher price tag than the old model — but the app is still a bit tetchy. Still, this great-sounding bar is a great option for Sonos homes with living rooms too small for the Arc Ultra.

The Sonos Beam Ultra feels like a statement of intent. The app works better than ever, the sound is incredible, and the surround sound straight out of the bar itself is top-notch. There are still problems — music sounds bad, and a lack of HDMI passthrough is a shame.

But this is Sonos on top form. The design is great, bringing that Sonos minimalism to a smaller bar than the enormous Arc Ultra. It’s perhaps a little more plain than some of the brand's other devices, but it's a handsome thing that’ll blend in perfectly with any living room decor. The traditional black and white colorways are still the only options, unfortunately.

And then there’s the way it sounds. It increases the Dolby Atmos effect with height channels, making for a more immersive movie experience that lands you directly in the center of the action. Add in a few extra Sonos speakers for a full surround setup and you have the perfect movie-watching experience for a smaller space.

It is expensive, mind you. The Beam was never cheap, but this one ups the price ante to make it a less compelling buy than other bars around this size class. And while Sonos app is much better than it was in early 2025, I’ve had more problems with it than our tester, with dropouts and other problems.

Setup is super easy. You just plug the soundbar into a wall outlet, and then an HDMI cable into the eARC port on the back of your TV. That could be it, if you’re not interested in any of the extra Sonos features.

To finish setup you’ll need to use the Sonos app, which is now much improved. From there you can do sound tuning setup amongst other things, like connecting extra Sonos surround speakers or a subwoofer for extra bass. It’s simple and easy to do, and the app will take you through it step by step.

This is also where you’ll stream audio to the device or adjust any settings. There’s no remote that comes with the soundbar — everything goes through the Sonos app.

The Beam Ultra really stretches the “compact” soundbar thing. It measures around 30 inches wide, making it a larger soundbar than some of the smaller compact options. That makes it perfect for TVs around 55 inches and smaller, though Sonos says it works for TVs up to 65 inches.

For larger spaces and TVs you’ll want the larger Sonos Arc Ultra.

In the box, you’ll find the soundbar, a power cable, and the HDMI cable. That’s it. There’s no remote, no wall mount — just the soundbar.

You can buy extras. Sonos speakers, the Era 100, 300, Sub Mini and Sub 4 all work as surround options for the Beam Ultra. I’d recommend the Era 100 and Sub Mini for smaller rooms if you want to increase the surround capability of the bar.

Unfortunately, everything has to come from Sonos’ rather enclosed ecosystem. You cannot add a separate 3rd-party subwoofer, for example. Shame.

The Beam Ultra is the best Dolby Atmos soundbar for its size. There’s real height to the sound here, making for a far better immersive bubble than other similarly sized bars. There’s width too — it’s a great way to watch your favorite movies.

Unfortunately, stereo music sounds straight up bad. That’s a shame, given that Sonos nailed it with the Arc Ultra — if you want to listen to music, you’re better off grabbing a stereo pair of Era 100s. It’ll cost you less, too.

I've seen loads of soundbars pass over Tom's Guide's testing table, and while there are some excellent options out there, not all of them can fit onto one list.

That doesn't mean they're bad, by any stretch, and they might just be the best soundbar for you. Here are some of the soundbars that we liked testing but didn't quite make the cut for the main roundup.

For the same money as Sonos's Beam Ultra, the Marshall Heston 60 is another compelling compact option. It might not quite reach the same heady heights as the Beam Ultra for movie watching, but it absolutely obliterates the Sonos when it comes to listening to music. It's just a shame that there aren't any surround speaker options.

Samsung's biggest and most premium sound is very good, offering excellent Dolby Atmos out of the box thanks to its included subwoofer and surround speakers. If you're looking for an all-in-one package for a Samsung TV it's a great option, but we believe the JBL equivalent offers a more rounded surround experience. If you're looking for the best soundbar surround sound, then look for the more expensive Sonos setup.

This mid-range soundbar brings excellent sound, but it forgot to bring the premium price. You won't get any smart features, which is a shame, but when it sounds this good, you won't really care. The sub in the box is surprisingly strong for this price point, and the bar itself offers solid surround for the dollars you'll pay.

The KEF XIO is one of the best-sounding soundbars we've ever tested. It's also one of the best-looking and best-built. "So why isn't it on the list!?" Because it costs $2,500. While I let that sink in for a second, I'll also tell you that the app experience is hit or miss. Still, if you have the dollars lying around, there are far worse ways to spend thousands of smackeroos.

LG's Sound Suite Dolby Atmos FlexConnect (phew) technology is very cool, and in the right room it can sound very good. Unfortunately, its core sound simply isn't up to scratch when compared to the competition, and the Sound Suite FlexConnect speakers are sold separately for a hefty premium. A proof of concept that shows its worth waiting for the sequel — but it needs some more time in the oven.

The Polk Audio Signa S4 brings a great sound and surprisingly solid Dolby Atmos for a decent price. The included sub is plenty bassy, and there's good spaciousness to the sound. It's a large bar despite its lower price. The comprehensive remote control is comfortable and easy to use.

If you want something that looks super sleek and tidy, then the True X Bar is a great option. Its Dolby Atmos performance is admirable, and the price is right. We reviewed the 40A, but you can find the 50A for around the same price now. It's exactly the same, but comes with a subwoofer. But you can also buy the 40A and add a subwoofer later.

Read our full Yamaha True X Bar 40A review

One of the best bits of most modern soundbars is that they're all simple to use in some form or another — but if you want something that you just plug in and use, then you'll want to avoid any with smart features.

While those smart features can make them sound better, or work for different types of content, they add complexity. An app might make it possible to access room EQs and the like, it also makes it more complicated for the end user.

Although we used to recommend avoiding Wi-Fi connections and apps if you just want to plug in and play, almost all soundbars now have some smart features. So I'd recommend looking for models that don't solely rely on those if the physical connection is your main focus.

First up, if your primary use case is music, go for a pair of speakers with an HDMI port like the Fluance Ri71. They sound much better than soundbars for music. You'll thank me later.

Now, for the other questions. TV users will want something that increases dialoge clarity and makes it easier to hear what's going on in the news. You won't need a subwoofer or any kind of surround support. The Sony HT-S100F above is going to be perfect for you, given it's not too expensive and works great for TV.

Movie watchers should look out for subwoofers and surround speakers. You want more space for your Dolby Atmos mixes and the subwoofer will help with the low-end rumble you get with movies. The Sonos Arc Ultra and subwoofer is a good option for you, or the JBL Bar 1300XMK2 if you want something in one package.

If you have a small room or use a small TV, you don't want a massive soundbar; that much should be obvious. It wouldn't fit, for one, but it would also make your TV look much smaller. And who wants that.

However, you also don't want a soundbar that's too small for your TV. Otherwise, all of the sound will appear to come from the middle of the TV, rather than from it's sides like it should.

You'll want to get a decently sized soundbar if you've got something between 50-75 inches big. Larger than that and you should probably consider either the biggest soundbar you can lay your hands on, or a proper stereo setup built around one of the best home cinema receivers.

The two pre-paired wireless surround speakers can be positioned behind or beside your seating area, while two bass drivers built into the 32-inch soundbar mean you don’t need a separate subwoofer.  The system maxes out at 95 dB, with bass extending to 50 Hz.

If your current TV sound setup is lacking some oomph and you want an under-$100 upgrade with a subwoofer and soundbar, the Vizio 4.1 Pro SV410YW-10 Soundbar and wireless surround speaker combo is a good choice for the money.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

#3198. Walmart’s 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales Are Live

If you're thinking of picking up any big-ticket items—whether for yourself or as a gift for someone on your list—I would advise you not to sleep on Walmart's sale. Walmart was the first major retailer to announce and kick off its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale for 2026, and they're holding three major shopping events through the December holidays.

Walmart will hold three sales between Nov. 12 and Dec. 2, as outlined in a recent press release. The sales will be both online and in-store, and will target a mix of Walmart+ members and general shoppers.

The events will take place on three different dates:

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 1: Nov. 12–15

Available online and in stores starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access beginning online at 12:01 a.m. ET on Nov. 12

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 2: Nov. 23–29

Online only: Nov. 23 starting at 12:01 a.m. ET

Online and in stores: Nov. 27 starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access online beginning Nov. 23 at 12:01 a.m. ET

Walmart's Cyber Monday Deals Event: Nov. 30-Dec. 2

Walmart's physical stores will open at 6:00 a.m. local time on Nov. 27 for their Black Friday events. Of course, they will start online earlier, so make sure to check their website as well.

Walmart says that they will have discounts on electronics, toys, fashion, beauty, home goods, gifts, and everyday essentials. Although the company doesn't provide much in the way of specifics in its press release, last year's sales included discounts on TCL TVs, Dyson vacuums, Dreo appliances, and toys from LEGO.

Walmart's first sale already features plenty of good deals; you don't need to wait for Nov. 27 to start to find some products going for their lowest prices ever. Here are some of the best ones I've found so far:

No. But if you are a Walmart+ member, you'll get early access to the sale. You can sign up for a free 30-day Walmart+ subscription and cancel it afterwards or get the annual plan for $98 ($8.17/month).

Deals are both online and in the physical stores. There might be deals online that you won't see in-store and vice versa.

The holiday season will see major sales from the same list of retailers that compete for your dollars throughout the year—namely, Best Buy, Target, and Amazon. Each will have its own version of Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales. So far, only Walmart has revealed its plans.

In short, yes. Though they aren't quite as impactful as they once were, Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales offer discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Whether it's a major purchase you've been saving up for or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts, especially on items like appliances and electronics. Last year's sales included categories such as tech, home improvement, and fitness.

Black Friday used to be when major retailers offered their best deals on expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Now, however, the distinction is almost meaningless: Every major retailer offers sales on both days, which means the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers to monitor the deals, and refer to our Black Friday coverage, where we do all the searching, curating, and price tracking for you.

#3197. Apple TV hit comedy from Ted Lasso, Shrinking creator returns next week

Apple TV (now $6.99/month for Black Friday) has a new season of hit comedy Bad Monkey coming next week from Bill Lawrence, co-creator of Ted Lasso and Shrinking. Here’s what Lawrence says to expect from Bad Monkey season 2.

Among Apple TV comedies, three of the best share one creative force behind them: Bill Lawrence.

When you're pumping weights or running a marathon, you're going to want something to keep your mind occupied — and there's little better than the best workout headphones. Listen to music, catch up with your favorite podcast, or devour some of an audiobook. Whatever you're doing you'll need some buds.

There are loads of options out there, but some are better than others. Our favorites are the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2, with their great sound perfectly pairing with solid ANC and a comfortable fit.

We've tested plenty more of course, and we've tested as many as we can. So read on to find out which headphones you should be getting for your next sweat-proof listening session.

AI seems to be the latest fitness trend, popping up in smartwatches, workout apps, and headphones. I wouldn't recommend picking up a new pair of earbuds for these features. My experience is the AI functions aren't very useful, and will likely change a lot in the next few years. So, focus on finding a set that feel and sound good, allowing you to focus on your exercise without distraction.

For a long time, Beats headphones didn't make me think of exercise. But that was before Apple redesigned the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 in early 2025 into what are effectively AirPods for workouts, with active noise cancellation (ANC), an effective transparency mode, and proper support for iPhone and Android devices.

The winged design of the older Powerbeats Pro has been replaced with over-ear hooks, which are a lot more stable. I'd sometimes need to fiddle a bit to get them on, but once locked into place, they didn't budge. And because the hook keeps some of the weight out of your ear, they were comfortable to wear for hours at a time.

Though the downside of this design is that the case is pretty big, and much larger than you'd comfortably fit into leggings or a pocket; fine for throwing in a gym bag, less ideal for carrying about, unlike the minuscule Beats Solo Buds case. But this one tops the battery up to 45 hours, while the Solo Buds case is just for storage.

The Powerbeats Pro 2 come with Apple's H2 chip, just like the AirPods Pro 3, so expect similar speedy performance, although I didn't find the noise cancellation or transparency mode were quite up to the flagship buds' standard. Though I did jump with delight at the use of physical buttons on each bud.

These headphones powered me through weights workouts, meditation sessions and long outdoor walks with no issues. I put them in and they did exactly what I wanted; good audio with no fuss. I don't run, but my coworker Nick Harris-Fry does, and found the Powerbeats Pro 2 a good companion for runs too.

The company leaned heavily into the buds' heart rate monitor at launch. It's neat, but you'll probably never use it. There's a small optical sensor built into the buds which is used to track your heart rate during workouts, but if this is something you care about, you likely have a smartwatch or Garmin watch that can do this better.

If you’re looking for some top-notch earbuds for working out that won’t break the bank, then look no further than the CMF By Nothing Buds 2. With loads of gym-centric features at a price that’s less than a fifth of some of the more expensive options on the list, they’re a fantastic way to keep fit while listening to tunes. Or a podcast. Or like, white noise. Whatever floats your workout boat.

At this price point, you wouldn’t expect to find anything with noise canceling, let alone ANC that works this well. It did a great job of keeping a noisy office at bay, so the pounding techno in the gym will be no problem. Outdoor runners, rejoice, they also blocked out traffic sounds when our tester, Ashley, took them out for a walk.

You don’t have to worry about your sweaty ears destroying them either, thanks to IP55 water resistance. You won’t be able to wear them while swimming, but anything you might get up to around your block or at the gym is no problem at all. Music, come rain or shine.

You don’t even have to worry about them running out of juice mid-workout. The quoted battery life from CMF is 12 hours — we found that around 5 hours of use left us with 60% remaining. Add in the 55 hours in the case, and you’re home free for super lengthy sessions.

They’re a little cheap-looking and the environmental noise canceling in calls is… not great. But then you look at your bank balance, realize that choosing the cheaper earbuds has left you with spare cash for a better gym subscription, and suddenly everything seems to make sense again.

They go in your ears, stay there, and play music while you get on with your workout. Better yet, they’ve done it for less than just about anything else around. What more could you want?

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are the follow-up to our former favorite running headphones, the OpenRun Pro. These bone conduction headphones sound great, despite the fact they use vibrations on your cheeks to transmit audio.

While out running with the OpenRun Pro 2 (or most Shokz headphones for that matter), we found that the fit was comfortable and secure, so you won't need to continually fiddle with them and can focus on your training.

The downside to the headband-style design is that you can't adjust the fit. However, there's a smaller edition (OpenRun Pro 2 Mini) that has a shorter band for improved fit. But we were impressed with the comfort during runs, bike rides, and yoga sessions.

You don't get a charging case, but we found that the battery would last around 12 hours between top-ups, which should see you through most workouts. That said, if you like to dial up the volume to max, expect closer to 10 hours of power.

I'm not a runner, but my multi-marathoner coworker Nick Harris-Fry summed up his feelings on the headphones, concluding: "They’re my preferred running headphones at the moment because of the excellent fit, open design and good sound. If you just want running headphones with an open design, it’s the OpenRun Pro 2."

They can survive sweaty workouts and light rain, but if you plan to train in the wet or want a more multi-functional set that'll cope with a dip in the pool, the OpenSwim Pro are a good alternative, and they have onboard MP3 storage.

The AirPods Pro 3 are Apple's newest flagship headphones, and stuffed with more features than ever. There's live translation, voice isolation on calls and head gestures to control your phone. All of that's great, but it's the fitness features that really stand out.

Like the Powerbeats Pro 2, the AirPods Pro 3 now have built-in heart rate sensors. Unlike the Beats set at launch, you can actually use the sensors with a load of different apps, including (importantly) Apple Fitness.

The new integration with Apple Fitness adds Workout Buddy, an AI-powered 'coach' which sends you motivational messages and performance stats, like an audio-only version of what you'd find on the Apple Watch Series 12.

I'm generally skeptical about features like this, but our resident marathon runner, Nick Harris-Fry, actually seemed impressed with the heart rate accuracy, which informs a lot of the performance metrics on Workout Buddy and Apple Fitness.

Then there's the fit. Despite being popular workout earbuds, I've always found that AirPods need quite a lot of fiddling to keep them in place. But that's not the case with the redesigned tip here, which Fitness Editor Jane McGuire said performed brilliantly on runs.

Despite being one of the first mainstream brands to launch water-resistant phones, the AirPods Pro 2 were surprisingly vulnerable, with just an IPX4 rating, essentially for splashes. The Pro 3 upgrade to a much hardier IP57 for dust and water resistance, so you can finally use them in the elements.

Like the AirPods Pro 2 before, the Pro 3 are still disappointing on the battery front: eight hours per bud, up to 24 hours with the case (while you got 30 out of the case on the Pro 2). It's not terrible, but the sub-$50 CMF By Nothing Buds 2 reach 12 hours.

The main reason I don't rate these higher in the list of best workout headphones is mostly due to the design — these aren't made for sports and they're not as secure a fit as you'd need for all high-intensity workouts. But for general use with your iPhone, including yoga, HIIT sessions, and casual runs, they're a great choice.

As Google continues to develop the Pixel-branded ecosystem of devices to rival Apple's iPhone and AirPods, it's no surprise that the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 are the best workout headphones for Android, even if they are targeted squarely at owners of the brand's range of Pixel phones.

The key upgrade from the first-generation Pixel Buds Pro is the addition of Google Gemini, the brand's generative AI model. As it's still fairly new, it doesn't replace the older virtual Google Assistant, although in theory it can. But in practice, we found that it doesn't always offer the most accurate answers.

Features like voice assistants and hands-free controls are useful, but not essential when you're working out. Instead, it's more important that they stay in place as you exercise. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 have a new wing on each bud to help them lock into your ears.

This would be great, but it doesn't quite reach the inner-top part of your ear, so we still found a bit of adjustment was needed to keep them in position for optimal noise cancellation. Google also claims to have improved the ANC, but it's hard to really tell the difference between the Pixel Buds Pro 2 and the original.

However, it's still effective, blocking out most noises except for some higher frequency sounds like crying babies and emergency service sirens. The sound quality matches the Pixel Buds Pro, although you may want to tweak the EQ to your preferences, as the default setting is a bit heavy on the lower end.

One other thing they have in common with the AirPods Pro is that they're not necessarily the best workout headphones if you spend hours training every week, as the fit isn't quite optimized for high-impact exercise. But if you're after a versatile option to wear at the gym and at the office, the Pixel Buds Pro 2 are a great choice.

Bone conduction headphones are cool, but they’re bulky. Your common earbuds sound great, but they have a habit of making it difficult to hear your surroundings. Open earbuds, like the Beyerdynamic Amiron Zero, are a great middle ground that offer solid sound while allowing you to hear the rogue bus that’s bearing down on you as you do your morning run.

They’re surprisingly secure, their silicone “hinges” holding onto your outer ear with little discomfort and no wiggle. Ashley, our tester, had no problem wearing them for hours and hours on end, partly thanks to their lightweight design. Just remember that these are completely open, playing the sound at your ears rather than in. Everyone is going to hear your playlist. Everyone.

The battery life could be better. There are 20 hours total on tap here, which falls down compared to in-ear options. You’ll be reaching for the charging cable more often than not, unfortunately, although you won’t need to pop them in the charging case as often with 6 hours of realistic listening time. Our tests pretty much confirmed this number.

Sound-wise, these are a great alternative to in-ear buds. There’s less bass than we might like overall, but there’s little else we’d ask for. The mids sound good, and the treble is solid as well. Don’t expect game-changing audio, but for open buds these sound great.

Even better, you can change the EQ. That’s a big bonus for something like this, and it means you can change the sound to your heart's content so that they sound great no matter your sonic preference. Five bands of adjustment, baby.

They’re IP54 water- and dust-resistant too, so you don’t have to worry about your sweaty ears causing any problems down the line. These are a good pair of earbuds that open you up to safer, more aware exercise — we really like them.

The workout headphones in the guide above aren't the only ones we've tested. We regularly try out workout earbuds so that we can recommend the top options that are worth spending your hard-earned cash on.

However, there are several other good options if you're after a bit more choice. These are the earbuds we've tested that didn't quite make the cut.

I really, really like these headphones. They're almost the perfect version of Beats' workout headphones, but the fit (ahem) isn't always perfect, and when they're only $50 less than the much more stable Powerbeats Pro 2 with fewer features and worse battery life, you're better off with the Pro 2.

Read our full Beats Powerbeats Fit review

The OpenFit Air 2 are great open earbuds, featuring solid sound and a comfortable fit. What holds them back from a full mention on the list is the fiddli-ness of the ear hooks — the clip-on design is superior if you're looking for something both secure and easy to wear.

When Apple launched these in mid-2024, I loved them, even though they didn't have noise cancellation or a charging case. But now these are only marginally cheaper than the much better Powerbeats Fit, and about the same price as the more feature-packed CMF By Nothing Buds 2, it's hard to recommend them.

The JBL SoundGear Sense have an open-ear design, so they sit on top of your ears rather than in them. We found this was fine for quiet environments or working out at home, but as soon as there was a lot of background noise from wind or traffic, it'd easily drown out the audio. They're comfortable and durable, but best-suited to indoor exercise.

Before investing your money in a set of workout headphones, you want to be sure that they do what they claim and are comfortable enough to wear during your training. That's why we put each set to the test before including it in the guide.

I've been testing headphones for almost ten years and know the most important areas to check out before recommending any pair. You really don't want them to fall out and get lost or need to continually adjust them in your ears.

So, we wear the headphones across a range of training styles, including high-impact runs (which can cause a lot of vibration and movement), intense fast-paced workouts and weightlifting sessions to see how they fare.

If they easily stay in place, they glide through this test, but it's not a write-off if they do move — headphones that struggle with runs may still make great weights companions — so we move into other areas, like comfort and sound.

For longer sessions, including runs, yoga classes and extended gym sessions, we check that the headphones are actually comfortable in your ears and don't leave you with ear pain or pressure headaches, which can happen with some sets.

Likewise, you don't want them to run out of battery mid-session, so we check how the battery life stacks up to the manufacturer's specs. For earbuds, we see how long they last out of the case and confirm how long the case can boost that.

When it comes to sound quality, even the best workout headphones aren't going to be a match for the best audiophile headphones in terms of clarity and detail. But that doesn't mean you need to put up with poor or low-quality audio.

We use a consistent playlist of music to help compare the headphones to other sets we've tested, which includes a variety of motivational dance music, dynamic rock songs, and everything in between, including the best new workout music.

There are a lot of Bluetooth workout headphones out there, so it can be a challenge to decide between them all. However, there are a few considerations to keep in mind that'll help narrow your options down to the right ones for your needs.

Firstly, it's vital that they stay in place during your exercise sessions. Some have ear hooks to physically hold them down, but others rely on clever engineering, a range of ear tips, or a specific set of materials to stop them falling out.

You also want them to survive some degree of moisture. If you plan to get sweaty, then you'll need a set rated to at least IPX4 for water resistance. But for outdoor workouts with a chance of rain, it's best to aim for an IPX7 rating.

Importantly, they also need to last the length of your workout. If you're doing short, high-intensity sessions, then you may only need an hour of battery. But with the right case, you may only need to recharge them every couple of weeks.

If long runs are more your thing or you're training for a marathon, you'll need a long-lasting set, like the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2, which are specifically designed with long distance outdoor runners in mind and last up to 12 hours.

And, finally, how loud do you like your workouts? If you don't mind some background noise at the gym, then a set of passive noise-canceling headphones should do the job, but most of the best workout earbuds have active noise cancellation (ANC) instead.

Earbuds with ANC cancel out the sound before it even hits your ears, so they're ideal if you want to zone out to your favorite tracks and focus on your exercise. But you may also want to hear traffic when you're out and about, so choose a set with a transparency mode too, which cancels most, but not all, noise.

In mid-2025, I had to do something hard; say goodbye to the Jabra Elite 8 Active. These were my favorite workout earbuds, but Jabra decided to focus only on business audio and no longer makes consumer earbuds or headphones.

I'd been using Jabra's Elite Active headphones since 2019, and for more than half a decade they comfortably sat atop my list of the best workout headphones. But we move. Times have changed, and they're gone (but still supported, for now).

You'd struggle to find a new pair now as most retailers have run down their supplies, but if you're after new workout earbuds, and to my mind, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are a worthy successor (even if they do add an ear hook).

If you've been hunting for new workout headphones, you may have noticed that each set has an IP rating for water resistance. This stands for Ingress Protection, and it's a measure of how well the buds can stand dirt and water.

There's a standard format to the rating — IPXY — where X refers to the level of dust protection and Y relates to the device's water resistance. The dust protection runs from 0 to 6, while water ranges between 0 and 9.

Unless you're working out in very dusty environments, the dust protection is less relevant and most brands don't even test them against that part of the standard. Instead, you'll want to pay attention to the water rating.

Headphones with an IPX4 rating are protected against water, so will cope with sweaty workouts. However, if you want to run in the rain (or are worried about getting caught in a storm) then aim for a set with an IPX7 rating.

This means they can be submerged in water up to 1 meter deep for 30 minutes without damage. That doesn't mean you should take them swimming (you'll want some waterproof headphones for that) but dropping them in a puddle isn't going to do them any harm.

Our roundup only includes workout earbuds, but it's not uncommon to see some people train with over-ear headphones instead, especially at the gym. So, which should you wear for exercise?

Ultimately, it comes down to preference, but there are a few factors to consider. Over-ears use an adjustable headband to keep them in place, so they're not likely to move about, especially if you're lifting weights.

Even just a few years ago, in-ear buds weren't really designed with exercise in mind, so they'd often fall out or need a lot of fiddling to keep them in place. But the best workout headphones we've included here all have ways to overcome that challenge.

Some, like the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2, have ear hooks to hold them securely, while others use a combination of weight balance and grippy materials to prevent them falling from your ear mid-workout.

But many people also feel like a larger set of headphones will have longer battery life and sound better too. However, the performance gap has shrunk, so you can get impressive noise cancellation and battery life from workout earbuds now.

The downside to over-ears is that they're generally not designed for sweaty exercise. Many have leather ear pads, and these quickly wear with repeated movements and contact with sweat. You can replace them, but it's not ideal.

The earbuds are also lighter, so you're less likely to notice you have them in, while over-ear cans can start to press against your skull and contribute to tension headaches, unless they're specifically designed for comfort. Although that usually makes them less durable.

Generally, no. This is partly due to the intricate designs required to make small earbuds packed with batteries, sensors, and headphone components. But it's also because most brands don't prioritize repairability.

Many sets, like those in our best workout headphones roundup, are durable, so shouldn't get easily damaged. And since most offer some degree of water resistance, a bit of sweat or light rain shouldn't cause you any problems.

So any significant damage is going to come from accidents, like dropping a weight onto an errant bud. However, you may notice a drop in battery life in the longer term, which you usually can't do anything about.

The only way around this would be to pick up a set of the Fairphone Fairbuds 2, which may be the world's most repairable earbuds since you can replace seven parts, including the battery and outer shell.

All of the sets in our best workout headphones roundup are wireless and connect to your smartphone or other devices via Bluetooth. But you can still find wired sets, including the Apple EarPods, which look a bit like AirPods but with a cable and Lightning connector to plug into your iPhone.

Wired sets also tend to be cheaper, so you may be considering a set that you wouldn't need to worry as much about damaging or replacing. However, it's important to consider how you like to train before picking up a wired set.

To keep them connected, you'll need to have your phone somewhere on your body, either in a pocket, waistband or running phone holder. Consequently, there are two different devices moving at different times as you exercise; your earphones and your smartphone.

The movements are translated between them with the cable, so if you stretch your leg out, the cable tenses and may tug on your earphones, which could lead to them falling out.

Plus, if you're working out with weights or other equipment, there's also the risk that the wire will get tangled up, leading to the headphones falling out or the cable getting ripped.

Similarly, if you prefer to keep aware of your surroundings, you can use most wireless workout headphones in mono mode, with just a single earbud in while the other stays in the case. You don't have the same option for wired workout headphones.

Many runners would advise picking up a set of the best bone conduction headphones for running. Like the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 in our roundup, these use vibrating pads on your cheekbones to reproduce audio, leaving your ears free to pick up the sounds around you, like traffic and other people.

This is very helpful while out running, especially if you want to run safely in the dark. Although music can be a great motivator, you don't want to miss important alerts like emergency vehicle sirens or bikes coming up behind you.

Plus, it means that you're more aware of everything else going on around you, including other runners and pedestrians. And if you plan to run races, using bone conduction headphones allows you to chat with other runners and listen to music.

You can get similar effects with most of the best workout headphones, as transparency modes use the earbuds' built-in mics to elevate environmental noise, but bone conduction headphones also wrap around your head, so stay in place more effectively during high-impact activities like running.

If you want to prevent your earbuds falling out of your ears or slipping out of place, the first thing to consider if the type of exercise you want to do. For running and other high-impact activities like jumping, the most secure type of workout headphones are those with ear hooks.

These sit above your ear to prevent them moving or falling out, and so can cope more effectively with vibrations. This is also why many runners opt for a set of the best bone conduction headphones, since these wrap around your head to similar effect.

If you want more minimalist earbuds, then before you start your workout, you can adjust the silicone ear tips. Most sets come with a small, medium, and large replacement pair of tips so you can find the ones that fit your ear size the most.
