Denmark’s TV2 has dipped into the independent production market for an Acting Program Director as it seeks penance over the scandal around Truman Show-like reality series Everybody Loves Rasmus

Sune Roland will take up the position on December 1, and will lead the TV2 programming division during a period the network “is working to rebuild the Danish public’s trust.” Given his position is an acting role, it’s not certain he will be TV2’s long-term program chief just yet.

This follows the departures of Content Director Ulla Pors and Program Director Dorthe Thirstrup following the disastrous launch of Alle Elsker Rasmus (Everybody Loves Rasmus). Related Stories News Content Chiefs At Denmark's TV2 Step Down To "Restore Trust" After Backlash Over 'Truman Show'-Style Reality Series News Banijay Takes On Norway's 'The Comedy League'

The show faced immense public backlash for duping comedian Rasmus Wallbridge into believing his dream film concept was being produced. It was scrapped soon after launch, and TV2’s directors have launched an investigation into how the show was greenlit in the first place. Their response has been fast and decisive during in an almost unprecedented situation for a major European broadcaster. Watch on Deadline

Roland is a former TV2 exec, having risen as high as Head of Content, and returns after four years in the independent production sector. He had worked as Managing Director of Strong Productions, the Fremantle Denmark production house that merged with Blu last year. Following his exit there, he launched his own company, Shift Studios.

Frederik Lauesen, who was installed as Acting Content Director at TV2 in the aftermath of the scandal, said: “I am very pleased that Sune Roland has agreed to take on the role of Acting Programme Director. Sune brings extensive experience; he is well-liked and respected within the industry and possesses a deep understanding of both TV 2 and the Danish production landscape. He is a highly skilled professional and an accomplished leader, and we will greatly benefit from his expertise in the time ahead.”

Lauesen said TV2 was facing “a serious situation” and that rebuilding trust was paramount. “We must address this while continuing to manage a large and diverse portfolio of content – an effort we carry out in close collaboration with our talented colleagues in the programming department and the Danish production industry. Sune’s experience from both sides of the table will prove valuable in the time ahead.”

Roland acknowledged he was joining in “particularly challenging times,” but added: TV2 holds a special place for me, and I know how many talented and dedicated people work every day to create content that truly matters to the Danish public. I look forward to contributing my experience and collaborating with both colleagues and production companies.”

Roland worked as TV2’s Head of Factual between 2007 and 2011, and then from 2012 until 2022 held roles such as Head of Programming, Channel Head, and Head of Content. He has also held senior leadership positions at Koncern TV and Metronome Productions.

TV2 will begin a recruitment process for a “future leadership team within the programming division” at a later date.

#3189. You Can Get One of These Pocket E-Readers for As Little As $55 During Black Friday

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a big discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3188. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

Black Friday isn't until November 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday 2026 sale is already bringing some decent discounts on TP-Link routers, with prices starting at $44.99 and savings of up to $100. The deals cover quite a few different networking needs, from compact travel routers that let you connect multiple devices to hotel wifi to more powerful home routers designed for faster internet plans and households with lots of connected devices.

TP-Link’s Roam routers are compact enough to travel with and let you share a hotel or public internet connection across your devices through a private Wi-Fi network—and right now, Amazon has three models on sale: the Roam 6 AX1500 for $44.99 (was $59.99), the Roam 6 AX3000 for $55.98 (was $79.99), and the Roam 7 BE3600 for $87.99 (was $119.99). All three support VPN connections and multiple operating modes, with the main differences coming down to speed. The AX1500 offers up to 1.5Gbps, the AX3000 doubles that and adds a 2.5Gbps WAN port, while the Wi-Fi 7-enabled Roam 7 reaches up to 3.6Gbps.

The TP-Link Archer AX21 V5 AX1800 is down to $54.99 from $89.99, saving you $35 on an affordable Wi-Fi 6 router for everyday home use. Its dual-band connection offers combined theoretical speeds of up to 1.8Gbps, which should be sufficient for typical activities like streaming, video calls, and browsing across several devices.

For homes with faster internet plans, multiple gamers, or lots of connected devices, TP-Link's Archer BE700 and BE770 offer tri-band Wi-Fi 7, including access to the 6GHz band for compatible devices. Both support EasyMesh for extended coverage and have 10Gbps WAN ports, although the BE770 provides faster wireless speeds and more wired connectivity. As for pricing, the TP-Link Archer BE700 is down to $248 from $349.99, saving you just over $100. It offers theoretical speeds of up to 15Gbps, a 2.5Gbps LAN port, and three Gigabit LAN ports. For just $52 more, the Archer BE770 (now $299.99, was $369.99) bumps speeds up to 18Gbps and adds a dedicated 10Gbps LAN port, making it better suited to high-speed network storage and large file transfers.

The TP-Link Deco BE25 is down to $99.98 from $129.99, saving you $30 on a Wi-Fi 7 router designed to work as part of a mesh network. It offers dual-band wireless speeds of up to 5Gbps, two 2.5Gbps Ethernet ports, and AI-driven roaming that helps connected devices switch between Deco units as you move around your home.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

#3186. These are the 4 best streaming devices we've tested to upgrade your TV

Get the most out of your TV using one of the best streaming devices

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The best streaming devices are a relatively cheap way to upgrade your TV's streaming capabilities. If you have a non-smart TV, these HDMI-attached dongles and boxes mean you can use it to stream from all your favorite apps. But they're also a good option if you have a great TV with older software.

For most people, the best streaming device is the Roku Streaming Stick Plus. It has an app store, easy access to all your services and won't break the bank. If you're after a more polished experience (especially if you own an iPhone), then the Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) is your best bet, but it'll set you back a lot.

These two are not your only options, though. We've tested the best streaming devices available right now, including options from Amazon and Google, to help you upgrade your home viewing experience without breaking the bank, and saving you from needing to replace a perfectly good TV just to get new software.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Roku's streaming devices have topped this list for a long time, and the latest Roku Streaming Stick Plus is only going to cement the brand's place at the top of the tree. The Streaming Stick Plus has loads of features that make it the best option around right now, from fantastic 4K streaming to a simple, slick UI.

This compact wonder brings powerful streaming without taking up loads of room behind your TV. Roku's user interface is among the best around, making searching through your favorite streaming services a breeze. The Roku remote that comes with it isn't the fanciest, but it's well laid out and simple to use, and supports voice commands.

The most important part, of course, is how good it makes your TV shows look. And, despite its lower price, we're happy to report that the 4K output is excellent. We combined it with a Samsung OLED TV, and it looked about as spectacular as you might expect.

Roku has slipped in some funky extras as well. We really like the screensavers — called Backdrops — that play when you're not using the TV. It avoids image retention and burn-in, which is a bonus, but it also makes what could be a big, black rectangle in your room something that actually adds to the decor.

The biggest drawback is the pesky ads. Make sure you turn off video autoplay, lest you be bombarded by irritating, noisy videos on startup. The ads are otherwise relatively easy to ignore. Despite the annoying ads, the Roku Streaming Stick Plus is an excellent streamer.

It's forty bucks. That's the pitch. It's just about the cheapest way to make your aging TV into a streaming powerhouse. There are fewer bells and whistles, and it doesn't have the highest resolution, but it doesn't cost much and means you can watch Amazon Prime, Netflix and more on your TV.

There are more features than you'd expect, though. While you won't get 4K, you do get some more premium sound formats like Dolby Atmos, should you be hooked up to a surround sound system. There are HDR formats galore as well, so the 1080p image will be super clear and colorful.

It's easy to set up and works speedily with the included remote control. It's not fancy, but it's cheap. And if you want to get the cheapest and easiest way to get streaming, there's not much better. Just don't bother if your TV is a smart TV — the built-in streaming is better.

The Google TV Streamer is a huge improvement over the old Google Chromecast. Similar functionality and navigation remain — and now you get live TV integration, tons of free content, plus several live TV services to choose from (YouTube TV, Sling and Philo).

But now, it also packs 4K UHD streaming with support for HDR and Dolby Vision for excellent picture quality, and Dolby Atmos for immersive sound. And with Google TV, you have support for over 6,500 Android TV apps.

That's not all, as the TV Streamer has a slew of smart home integrations that make it stand out. Directly from your TV, you can now monitor and control all your smart home devices.

We were able to view live streams from our various home security cameras and video doorbells, and also see which lights were still on — and dim them, too. You can even check the temperature on your smart thermostat. It's a step up from what other streaming devices offer and will make smart home enthusiasts gush the world over.

As with most newer TV models, Google has also incorporated its Gemini AI into the TV Streamer. This will do a variety of tasks, like providing simple summaries of whatever content is on-screen and pulling in reviews from both critics and the general public — for better or worse.

You can also use Gemini to create screensavers. Think of (almost) anything and speak it into the remote, and Gemini will create it for you, to amusing (or horrifying) effect.

One of the most surprising things about the 2026 Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) is not that it now comes with AI, but that it is twice the price of the 2022 version. That's an incredible jump in cost, even considering the price hikes we've seen across all areas of our lives. Whether it's justified depends on how much you use Apple's services.

Taking price out for a moment, the experience of using the Apple TV 4K is fantastic. It's uncluttered and easily links up to your non-Apple streaming apps like Netflix. Of course, one of the main attractions is how seamlessly it integrates with Apple's services and hardware, which is why it's the best streaming device for iPhone owners too.

Which brings us back to the price. Unless you have an iPhone or heavily use the Apple TV streaming service, it's probably not worth the investment. But the quality-of-life features you get with an iPhone make the price easier to swallow. Some of the smallest features on tvOS (Apple's software) are actually the best.

The included Siri remote uses an iPod-like touch scroller, which is great for navigation but pretty useless for text entry. So when you tap a text box, an Apple TV keyboard pops up on your iPhone, so you can easily enter usernames and passwords. But in theory, the biggest addition to the 2026 model is Siri's Apple Intelligence upgrade.

It's not hugely exciting, but it is a step up from Classic Siri. We tried Classic and AI Siri voice commands, asking for lists of movies with certain actors. Classic wouldn't get it right, but AI-powered Siri did just what we asked. It's good, not great, and depending on your views on AI, might not be worth twice the price of the 2022 edition.

We test streaming players by looking at both the content they can provide (most are very similar at this point) and how they deliver said content. Any streaming player worth its salt can load a 4K stream, but only a good one possesses straightforward navigation, robust search features and a wide variety of content to suit all tastes.

The first thing we evaluate is the setup, to see how quick and simple it is. From there, we take the user interface for a spin to see what content gets highlighted, what gets hidden, and how easy it is to navigate to our favorite channels.

As live TV service integration becomes a bigger feature in streaming devices, we look at how these sticks and boxes can place your favorites within closer reach.

We'll also watch a few different shows on a variety of channels to gauge the quality of the video and audio, to make sure they look good regardless of whether you have one of the best TVs or not.

After that, it's onto the extra features, like gaming, voice search and screen mirroring. These factors don't weigh quite as heavily toward the final score, but they're nice to have if they work well, and extremely distracting if they don't.

The main reason to get a streaming stick is that your TV is either missing a feature you want, or you'd rather not replace a perfectly good television just because it doesn't connect to the internet and download apps.

These are both great reasons to invest in these small and relatively inexpensive devices. After all, even the best TVs under $500 are still a strain on your bank balance, and if there's nothing wrong with your existing set, why send it out to the trash when you don't need to?

But if you buy a TV, you'll end up using the software that comes installed on it. With the best streaming devices, you have a lot more choice. Roku, Amazon, Google and Apple all have great options that you can use on any TV, and you don't have to be invested in each ecosystem to enjoy them (though it can help).

Generally speaking, the cheaper devices are supported by ads or feature-locked subscriptions/upgrades. But if you want to get what I'd argue is the best streaming device for iPhone owners (that's the Apple TV 4K), you'll need to spend more, but it's an entirely uncluttered, ad-free experience.

Although for other tech devices, there'd be a lot more between them, the choice here really comes down to price, brand and software. All the devices we've featured have apps for the major streaming platforms, so you won't miss out. Not that I really recommend AI, but the Google TV Streamer is ideal if you're a big Gemini user.

Or if you want to go the other way, I'd advise the Apple TV 4K — not because it doesn't have AI (the 2026 box has the new AI Siri experience), but because it's not that interesting, so you won't ever feel compelled to use it. I'm being a little unfair; it works with Apple's own services, but it's less reliable for third-party apps and services.

#3185. WhatsApp launches highly requested new feature for sending messages later

WhatsApp just announced that it is rolling out scheduled messages, which it says is one of users’ most requested features. Here are the details.

From WhatsApp’s blog post announcing support for scheduled messages:

You can write a message when you think of it and send it anywhere from 10 minutes to 14 days later, in both your 1:1 and group chats.

To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It will look like any other message to the person receiving it. You can see all future messages you have lined up, and delete them beforehand if you change your mind.

Even if your phone is off or out of battery, your scheduled message will still show up at the time you chose, and it remains end-to-end encrypted like all your personal messages, so no one else can read it, not even us.

WhatsApp says this feature is “rolling out globally over the coming weeks.” So you might not see it right away, but even if you don’t, it should show up on your account soon.

Scheduled messages work not only for text, but also when sending media like photos and videos.

To get access to scheduled messages, make sure you’ve updated to the latest WhatsApp app update, which was just released today.

In other WhatsApp news, earlier today we reported that stickers with audio are coming soon, including user-created options.

What are your top feature requests for WhatsApp? Was scheduled messages on that list? Let us know in the comments.

#3184. ‘Sunrise On The Reaping’ Firing Up Thanksgiving With $85M+ 5-Day; ‘Focker In-Law’ & ‘Hexed’ Fight For 2nd With $35M+ Apiece – Update

THANKSGIVING AM UPDATE: An alpha female property, Lionsgate‘s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping with a continued 5-day forecast of $85M+, is stealing business from two other female-leaning movies at the Thanksgiving box office, Universal/Paramount’s Focker In-Law and Disney’s Hexed, both of which are coming in lighter than their forecasts with 5-days of $36M and $35M respectively. That’s essentially a fight for 2nd over the Wednesday-Sunday stretch at this point in time.

Now, that’s not to say that it was silly to date other female pics on top of another tentpole, however, the holiday has shown that two exceptionally pleasing events for the demo can coexist at the same time, read 2024’s Moana 2 and Wicked and even last year’s Wicked: For Good and Zootopia 2. Hexed and Focker In-Law aren’t exceptionally pleasing.

Most movies are expected to ease on average -23% today off their Wednesday daily B.O. as families ease back for festivities. Tomorrow, Black Friday, should see a daily surge between 50%-100% for most titles. Watch on Deadline

Sunrise on the Reaping‘s $15.1M Wednesday is the second best in the Suzanne Collins’ franchise after 2013’s Catching Fire which did $20.8M on the day before Thanksgiving. 3-day is still on track for $58M+, -51%.

Focker In-Law saw an uptick in its franchise CinemaScore to B+ from previous chapter, 2010’s Little Fockers which received a B-. The original movie 26 years ago has the best grade of A-. The pic is alright with a 64% definite recommend in Screen Engine/Rentrak PostTrak exits. Yesterday was $5.3M with the 3-day at $24.8M. Half of the audience was 18-34 yesterday, 46% over 35 and 64% female overall. Diversity demos were 37% Caucasian, 33% Latino and Hispanic, 13% Black, 10% Asian American and 7% Native American/other. PLFs rep 17% of the gross so far with the John Hamburg directed sequel (the first two pics were helmed by Jay Roach, the third by Paul Weitz) playing best in the West, South, and South Central. AMC Burbank is the top venue with $21k. Again, the Uni and Paramount co-production cost $90M net before global P&A.

Disney’s $200M Hexed is waiting for a box office spell tomorrow that could raise this original animated movie above the doldrums of the studio’s Thanksgiving 2023 dud Wish ($175M production cost, $8.1M Wednesday, $19.6M 3-day, $31.6M 5-day and final domestic of $63.9M). Hexed made $7.6M yesterday (including Tuesday previews) and is eyeing a 3-day of $20M. Hexed gets an A- just like Wish did. PostTrak shows 62% definite recommend for the general audience while kids under 12 gave it a 96% in the top 2 and a 51% must see right away. Kids under 12 rep 31% of the audience while 35-44 (parents) showed up at 31%. Diversity demos were 48% Caucasian, 26% Latino and Hispanic, 9% Black, 7% Asian American and 9% Native American/other.

Again, there are no original songs in this movie about a mother and daughter witch, the latter who realizes her powers as both are transported into another portal where they are trying to save their own kind from doom.

Like Focker-in-Law, Hexed is sharing PLFs with Sunrise on the Reaping which owns most of the holiday supply, those screens are counting 17% of the animated pic’s holiday B.O. so far. 3D is driving 12%. West, South, South Central, Midwest and Mountain are the best markets with the East soft performing 2% below the norm this week. AMC Dine-In Disney Springs Florida is the best location with $52k.

Paramount’s Ebenezer is looking at 4th place at 3,180 theaters with $1.6M yesterday, and still $6.8M-$7.3M third weekend, -6% to -13%, for a 5-day of $10M-$10.6M and running cume on the high end of $45.9M.

Fifth is Amazon MGM Studio’s I Play Rocky with $1.4M yesterday at 2,711 sites, $6.6M 3-day, -29%, 5-day of $9.6M and total of $22.6M by EOD Sunday.

Outside the top 5 is Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth at 252 locations, boosted by AMC Imax. Wednesday’s opening day estimate was $910K, 3-day is looking at $3.3M and a 5-day of $4.85M. At that level, the theater average over 5-days is $19,2K which is higher than what Netflix pulled did last Thanksgiving with Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery which had a per theater of $7K. Note that Rian Johnson directed thriller was booked in more theaters at 600 sites. Still a bit more robust result here on a limited basis than Wake Up Dead Man ($4.25M 5-day), but alas, Netflix, you’re leaving soooo much money on the table and there’s more than a enough room in this marketplace to have gone wide and minted at least $20M for this sequel to beloved fan Quentin Tarantino pic Once Upon a Time in Hollywood which at $142.8M is the Oscar winning filmmaker’s second highest grossing movie at the domestic B.O. Cliff Booth filmmaker David Fincher told Collider that the pic cost $120M-$123M, not $200M. We’ll leave it to Wall Street to figure out the downstream.

There’s a shot that Neon’s third weekend wide expansion of James Gray’s crime noir, Paper Tiger, based on the filmmaker’s life, comes in higher than Cliff Booth. Wednesday was an estimated $950K which translates into a $4.4M 3-day, 5-day of $5.1M at 1,322 (+1,294) theaters. Running total by Sunday is around $5.7M. Audiences weren’t wild about the Miles Teller, Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson movie giving it a C+.

Angel Studio’s Hershey biopic about the chocolate maker with Alexandra Daddario and Finn Whitlock got a leg up with early shows yesterday with $1.3M including $534K estimated previews. No firm projection yet, but it was always expected to file in the single digits over its ‘4-day’ start. The pic doesn’t officially open until Thursday and all that preview cash will be rolled into day one. CinemaScore audiences love it with an A, and PostTrak isn’t shabby with 83% positive and a 69% definite recommend, but critics didn’t have a sweet tooth for it 17% Rotten. Male-to-female turnout was 50/50 with the Angel faithful attending at 37% over 55, and 51% over 45. Diversity demos are 61% Caucasian, 17% Black, 13% Latino and Hispanic, 6% Asian American, and 3% Native American/other.

WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON: If extreme weather doesn’t shutter theaters in the Northeast, then Lionsgate is looking forward to a lucrative Thanksgiving stretch with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping potentially banking $85M+ over five-days.

Should the sixth title in the Suzanne Collins series file in that range, it will rep the second best Thanksgiving haul for a Hunger Games movie after Catching Fire‘s $109.9M Wednesday-Sunday turkey take 13 years ago. Sunrise on the Reaping‘s Wednesday is looking like $15.5M-$16.5M with a second 3-day weekend around $58M-$65M at 4,018 theaters, -46% to -51%. Five day forecasts are always a challenge for the industry to predict: Business dips on Thanksgiving then spikes on Black Friday, which is one of the most active moviegoing days of the year. By Sunday, we’re looking at a running cume for the Francis Lawrence directed movie of $233M domestic, which would be 40% higher than the lifetime cume on 2023’s Hunger Games: Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.

Second will either be Disney’s Hexed at 3,725 theaters or Universal/Paramount’s Focker-in-Law at 3,382 sites. Hexed is seeing around $7.8M today (including $2.1M previews), for a 3-day around $20M and 5-day between $35M-$40M. Let’s see if this picks up before passing complete judgement on this $200M original animation production, but it’s clear Hexed isn’t Coco or Frozen.

Focker In-Law is seeing a $5.2M Wednesday, 3-day of $24.8M and 5-day of $36.1M. No Rotten Tomatoes audience scores yet on either title.

Fourth goes to Paramount’s third frame of Johnny Depp Christmas movie, Ebenezer with $1.5M today at 3,180 sites and a 3-day between $6.8M-$7.3M, -6% to -13%, for a 5-day of $10M-$10.6M and running cume on the high end of $45.9M.

Fifth is Amazon MGM Studio’s fourth frame of I Play Rocky at 2,711 with $1.4M today, 3-day of $6.6M, and 5-day of $9.5M for a running cume of $22.5M.

Outside the top 5 is Netflix’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth at 251 locations with $1M today, $3M 3-day and 5-day of $5M.

WEDNESDAY AM: As we told you last night, Lionsgate scored its best Tuesday ever at the domestic box office with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping and the best ever for the Suzanne Collins franchise as the day raked in $15.98M.

2013’s The Hunger Games: Catching Fire owned the previous best Tuesday for the franchise with $15.96M. Running cume for the fifth Francis Lawrence movie is $148.1M and by Thanksgiving, Sunrise on the Reaping will surpass its previous 2023 chapter’s lifetime domestic B.O. of $166.3M.

As we told you, Sunrise on the Reaping will dominate the Thanksgiving Wednesday through Sunday stretch as the franchise has historically done before since 2013, this time with a floor of $70M+. Previously, the pics over Thanksgiving cooked up the following: Catching Fire ($109.9M), Mockingjay Part 1 ($82.6M), Mockingjay Part 2 ($75.9M) with Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes way behind ($42.2M).

Lionsgate has had back-to-back global hit openings this year with Sunrise on the Reaping last weekend at $226.1M WW and Michael with $218.8M. This has all happened under the administration and watch of Motion Picture Chairman, Adam Fogelson. Still no word out there whether or not Lionsgate rejected or accepted Legendary’s bid.

Walt Disney Animation’s Hexed came in with $2.1M, $100K above the $2M we were spotting yesterday. That preview figure is higher than Encanto ($1.5M previews, 5-day of $40.5M) and Wish ($1.8M previews including $500K Saturday sneaks; 5-day of $31.6M). No RT audience score yet, but critics were meh at 67% fresh. There is a chance that the traditional Disney pic comes in lower than its 5-day forecast of $40M-$45M as original animated titles are very challenging to launch in the streaming era, but you have to start some place.

Universal and Paramount’s Focker In-Law, which didn’t have previews last night, rather began showtimes at midnight, has more potential to hit its 5-day forecast of $45M given the Ariana Grande factor and the fact that audiences love the franchise. The first Meet the Parents 26 years ago was the fave among critics at 85% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Focker-in-Law isn’t the worst at 26%, as that belongs to 2010’s Little Fockers. 2004’s Meet the Fockers stands at 39%.

Hexed, Focker-in-Law and Sunrise on the Reaping are sharing PLFs with the latter having Imax screens (except for AMC where they are being designated to Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth).

Thank God for Lionsgate Hunger Games at the box office: Sans a Wicked, Moana and a Zootopia, the Thanksgiving box office will certainly be down from last year’s five day robust $290.3M, which was the fifth best ever. Moana 2 and Wicked led the holiday to its best haul ever with $424.9M.

With Black Friday deals in full swing, it's a good time to consider the tech you've been waiting to go on sale, including highly giftable tablets and e-readers. #3182. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

#3180. iOS 27.3 release date: Here’s when new iPhone features are coming

iOS 27.3 is coming soon, packed with new features for iPhone users. Here’s when to expect the next big iPhone software update.

If you follow Apple closely, the company’s software release patterns quickly become clear.

For example, iOS 27.2 launched late last month around the same time as releases in years past. The only difference is that normally iOS 27.1 would launch in late October rather than 27.2. But since Apple made iOS 27.1 exclusive to iPhone Duo, all software releases for the iOS 27 cycle will be off by one number—despite following the same timing as ever.

That means iOS 27.3 is up next, and its release should align with historic patterns for x.2 updates.

Apple has confirmed that iOS 27.3 will launch to all users in December once beta testing concludes.

To get more precise though, here’s a sampling of release patterns for comparable x.2 updates the last few years:

Based on this pattern, iOS 27.3 is expected to release by mid-December.

Apple always tries to ship its last software update of the year with a little buffer before taking a holiday break. That way if any major issues arise, the company can develop a quick fix and push it out before much of the company takes time off.

Expect to see iOS 27.3 launch as early as the week of December 7, or on Monday, December 14 at the latest.

iOS 27.3 is packed with lots of new features for iPhone users spanning various popular apps.

Here are some of the new features in iOS 27.3:

iPhone Duo also benefits from three exciting new features, including face unlock, Reachability, and a new setting to automatically lock the device when closed.

Finally, iOS 27.3 brings the first Apple Intelligence features to China—though Siri AI is still missing.

The best smartwatch is almost always the one that works with your phone. Over the past few years, brands have moved away from universal compatibility and toward platform-specific watches that will only work if you use a particular phone.

One of the remaining holdouts is Amazfit, which launched the excellent Active 3 Premium that works on iPhone and Android. It's half the price of Apple or Google's watches, but you wouldn't know it from its impressive fitness tracking features.

It's incredible value, but if you're looking for the closest integration you can get with your phone or smart features like emergency or health alerts, then I'd recommend the Apple Watch Series 12 (iPhone) or Google Pixel Watch 5 (Android) right now.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Amazfit Active 3 Premium is the smartwatch I recommend for most people, and not just because it works with whichever phone you have. It's a fantastic fitness-tracking watch that easily holds its own against the Apple Watch Series 12 and Google Pixel Watch 5, without locking you to a specific platform or phone.

It is also incredible value — coming in at around half the price of the two flagship watches — and all the features are free with no subscription (unless you need Zepp Aura, the sleep-focused AI wellness app that generates audio to relax you). It has offline maps, tracks more than 170 activities, and comes with built-in GPS.

It has a smaller footprint (wristprint?) than many other smartwatches, with a 1.3-inch display, compared to the 1.77- or 1.96-inch Apple Watch Series 12. It's not a huge amount on paper, but it makes a big difference, as it felt smaller and less noticeable on our wrist. It's a shame it doesn't come in a few more vibrant colors, though.

While you don't get the smarts of Apple and Google's watches (emergency alerts, on-watch calls, third-party apps), fitness and activity tracking is where the Active 3 Premium really shines, with metrics to rival the best Garmin watches, like heart rate, blood oxygen, stress levels, cycle tracking, sleep quality and skin temperature.

The data all syncs to your phone, and you can view it and get insights in the Zepp app, available for Android and iPhone. If you ever used a Fitbit before the Google takeover, the Zepp app is the closest thing to that now-gone experience; easy to understand, straightforward to use, and guides you through all the different metrics.

This is particularly helpful if you're just getting into running, as the running features on the Active 3 Premium are almost as detailed as those you'd find on Garmin watches, yet everything is explained clearly, even for more complex topics like your lactate threshold and ground contact time, which assess how your foot strikes the floor.

Amazfit says that the Active 3 Premium should last 12 days between charges. Like most other smartwatches, that doesn't work out in the real world; we found that it'd generally last just over a week or eight days. That's down a bit on the spec, but still miles ahead of the 24-hour battery life on the Apple Watch Series 12.

Apple, Google and Samsung refresh their watches every year. Normally, these are pretty small upgrades, so I often recommend buying the previous year's model. But not with the Apple Watch Series 12. For the first time in almost half a decade, Apple has given the watch a pretty big health-tracking update.

The most significant change is that there's a new, more accurate heart rate sensor. This powers a few other changes, like the Readiness score you can get each day. This is something imported from other running watches and is a measure of how you've recovered after activity and how to improve the score.

I've tested watches with this kind of score and haven't found it that informative, but I know our resident runners find it particularly helpful when training for races. The improved sensors also allow for continuous heart rate monitoring (ie all day), which was previously limited to just during tracked workouts.

These practical and useful changes were only part of the Series 12 pitch. Apple also rolled out new AI Siri and a selection of 'helpful' AI-powered features, called Audio Intelligence. There are two (Live Rewind, Siri Recap), but both use the watch to capture speech around you and turn it into some form of recap.

Live Rewind is arguably the least helpful and most invasive. It listens to conversations (privately on your phone) and allows you to rewind live conversations in case you miss a detail, like someone's name (in case you were unaware you could ask the person to repeat what they said). Recap uses AI to summarize all that data into a journal-like, 'here's what happened today' note.

Honestly, these seem like gimmicks to me that very few people will ever use, and it normalizes surveillance. So, in case it wasn't clear, I wouldn't buy the watch for these and would jump into the settings to disable them. But in all other aspects, the Series 12 is the best Apple Watch you can buy right now and a worthy upgrade.

As with the Apple Watch, I wouldn't normally recommend the most recent version of the Google Pixel Watch, but this time I do think the Google Pixel Watch 5 is the better choice than the 4, but mostly because it's hard to find a new edition of the Pixel Watch 4 now that the Pixel Watch 5 exists.

That doesn't mean I don't think the Pixel Watch 5 is a great smartwatch — it is — but it's a relatively modest update this time around. But what you get for your money still makes it the best smartwatch for Android phones, especially if you own a Pixel device. And like Apple, it's the new health and safety features that are the headline.

The Pixel Watch 5 includes Breathing Emergency Detection, which is a lot like 2024's Loss of Pulse Detection, which uses the watch's sensor data to look for signs of a breathing emergency and automatically requests 911 support or trusted contacts for help. These two, along with Fall/Crash Detection, Blood Pressure Trends, and Insulin Resistance Trends, form part of Google's new "Health Guardian" suite.

Technologically, it's impressive. But do I recommend you buy the watch for them? I don't think so. It's a reassuring fallback if you do have an emergency, but you can't say with certainty that they'll always work as intended when you need them to. And reviewers (including us) can't really test them to check either.

What I like about the Pixel Watch range is that Google doesn't tie too many features exclusively to Pixel phones. The Pixel-exclusive features on the Watch 5 are: call screening, secure phone unlock, contact cards when someone calls you, and the ability to use your watch as a remote viewfinder for your phone's camera app.

The newest watch has also retained my favorite feature: repairable screens and replaceable batteries. This isn't as easy as popping the back off, but it makes the Pixel Watch 5 the most repairable smartwatch you can buy right now. iFixit even rated it a near-perfect 9/10 for repairability, while the Apple Watch Series 12 scored just 4/10.

It's not easy for me to praise Google (have you seen the Google Graveyard?), but it's a hugely positive move that saves you money in the long run and prevents otherwise good watches from going to the trash. But much of this was also true of the Pixel Watch 4, so if you can find a good deal on the older model, I'd go for that.

If you're after the best smartwatch for your phone, the three models I recommend above are going to cover most use cases, whichever phone you have. But there are a lot more smartwatches around right now.

Not every model can be the best, but some come pretty close. If you need a few more options, these are the smartwatches I still think are worth your money, and may fill a need we didn't cover in the wearables from Amazfit, Apple or Google.

Last year's Apple Watch Series 11 is so close to the older Series 10 that it does make you wonder why Apple released it, but for the first time in many years, there was a bump in battery life from 18 hours on the Series 10 to 24 hours on the Series 11. If you can get a good discount, it's a great option, but the Series 12 is a much better watch for not much more.

Read our full Apple Watch Series 11 review

The Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 generates free wellbeing insights from your data. This is a neat upside, as many other brands charge for this. The (potential) downside is that you need a Samsung phone to access them all in the Samsung Health app. But it's more expensive than the Galaxy Watch 8, despite modest changes and the same display. The Pixel Watch 5 is a better option unless you really need the Samsung integration.

Read our full Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 review

Apple didn't release a new budget watch in 2026, so the most recent is the 2025 SE 3. It's an excellent choice and has almost all the same features as the Series 10 and 11, minus some health-specific ones like ECG and blood oxygen monitoring. And like those models, it lacks the upgraded health sensors of the Series 12. If you can do without them, the SE 3 is a great value Apple Watch.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a useful update from the Ultra 3 with a redesigned, more accurate health sensor array and better battery life. It also comes with the same AI gimmicks as the Series 12. It's a good option if you need a larger, longer-lasting Apple Watch, but for most people, the Series 12 is the better (and cheaper) choice.

The Withings ScanWatch Light is a stripped-back version of the hybrid ScanWatch 2 I wear every day. It doesn't have a large color screen and is missing features like calls and apps, but it can track your activity, heart rate and workouts. I love the ScanWatch 2, and the compromise to reduce the cost is that the Light drops the flagship watch's health features, like an ECG. Otherwise, this is an excellent fitness tracking watch that'll last several weeks between charges.

Read our full Withings ScanWatch Light review

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is impressively cheap, retailing for less than most fitness trackers. It has a color display and two weeks of battery life; incredible at this price. But we found that step counts are inaccurate and the sleep tracking is unreliable. So I'd recommend the Amazfit Active 3 Premium instead.

Read our full Nothing CMF Watch 3 Pro review

We reviewed the first Apple Watch more than a decade ago, and we've been testing the best smartwatches ever since. The devices have gotten more complex, last longer and have way more features now, but the core of our testing has remained the same: we wear the watches, just as you would, to see how they hold up in the real world.

We look at how easy it is to set up, whether it has compatibility issues with specific phones and spending hours poking around in the software, looking for settings, apps and other features that make the device worth your money. Over the years, these watches have transitioned from phone companions to health and wellbeing trackers.

So we also focus on how these tools work, whether the tracking is accurate, how it compares to the competition and whether there's value in measuring what the company says you should. We wear the best smartwatches out on runs, during workouts, while sleeping and going about our day to see how they cope.

Over the past few years, brands have added more safety features to their watches, like irregular heartbeat notifications, sleep apnea alerts, crash and fall detection and hypertension alerts. These are things we can't practically test, so we can't verify that these work as intended or described.

In the U.S., health features are regulated by the FDA, so there is some degree of verification, but because we can't check that ourselves, I wouldn't recommend that you buy any of these watches specifically for these safety features. At the very least, they should be secondary to some other safety check.

It's not something you can predict, but sometimes a health issue does come along when you're testing a smartwatch. This happened to one of our writers — her Garmin watch alerted her to a potential heart problem she didn't know about, and that prompted her to go to the hospital to get checked out.

Before you go too far into your journey for a new smartwatch, first you need to work out which ones will work with your phone. The Apple Watch only works with iPhones, and some Android-focused watches have features that are exclusive to specific phones (I'm thinking of offerings from Google and Samsung here).

There are plenty of options that'll work with both platforms, but they generally aren't the flagship models that get a lot of attention every summer and fall, like the watch I rate as the best smartwatch right now, the Amazfit Active 3 Premium. It's more of a fitness smartwatch, but it can do a lot of what the others can do for a lot less.

And that's one of the other big choices you have to make: do you want a fitness watch that has smartwatch features, or a smartwatch as a companion to your phone that can track your fitness? These sound similar — and they are — but the difference is how much of the focus is put on either the smartwatch or fitness features.

Fitness smartwatches evolved from the best fitness trackers, with larger displays and more sensors. The best smartwatches started life as Bluetooth-connected extensions of your phone and over time became devices that keep you connected to your digital life, even when you're away from your phone working out.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Google Pixel Watch 5 are the best compromise between the two, but there are plenty of other options in our Also Consider section that also straddle that line or lean one way or the other. Though, if you need a cellular connection in your watch, those are pretty much limited to the flagship models.

#3177. Mark Tildesley Dies: ‘No Time to Die’, ‘F1: The Movie’ & London Olympics Production Designer Was 63

Mark Tildesley, one of the industry’s most respected production designers, has passed away aged 63.

Tildesley’s many credits include James Bond movie No Time To Die, 28 Days Later, The Constant Gardener, The Two Popes, Jay Kelly, Joseph Kosinski’s F1: The Movie, and Sam Mendes’ upcoming Beatles movies. Mendes today described his collaborator as “entirely original and extraordinarily gifted”.

Tildesley’s career spanned more than three decades and he collaborated with leading filmmakers including Danny Boyle, Richard Curtis, Michael Winterbottom, Martin McDonagh, Mike Leigh, Paul Thomas Anderson, Cary Joji Fukunaga, Ron Howard, Ben Wheatley, Oliver Stone and Mendes. Winterbottom and Mendes were among Tildesley’s most regular collaborators. With the former, he made seven films: I Want You, Wonderland, The Claim, 24 Hour Party People and Code 46. Boyle and Tildesley memorably teamed up for the 2012 London Olympics opening ceremony, a feat that earned the production designer an Emmy win alongside Suttirat Anne Larlarb.

With Mendes he made Empire Of Light and was aboard for the upcoming The Beatles — A Four-Film Cinematic Event alongside Stefania Cella and Neal Callow.

He won three British Film Designers Guild awards, for High-Rise, Empire of Light and F1: The Movie, as well as a Set Decorators Society of America prize, an Art Directors Guild award, and a British Independent Film Award.

Mendes said today: “Mark was a one-off: gentle, funny, warm, mischievous, entirely original and extraordinarily gifted. My abiding memory of him is from Empire of Light, flying down the Margate seafront on a motorised scooter, his technicolored scarf flapping in the wind, twinkling like a schoolboy playing hooky. A unique spirit and a wonderful artist. I am one of hundreds of people who are desperately sad that he is gone.”

The British Film Designers Guild (BFDG) said: “We are very sad to hear the news of Mark’s death. Besides being a well-respected and extremely talented production designer he was a friend and colleague to many of our members and will be very much missed by everyone in the Industry who knew and worked with him.”

#3173. Report: Apple gains ground as Latin American smartphone shipments plunge 24% in Q3

According to a new Counterpoint Research report, Apple increased its share of Latin America’s smartphone shipments in Q3 2026, recording the smallest decline among the region’s top five brands. Here are the details.

In a report released this week, Counterpoint Research says the ongoing memory crunch led to a 24% year-over-year drop in smartphone shipments during Q3, “the second-lowest quarter since 2015.”

Per the report, Samsung maintained its lead with a 35% shipment share, despite a 15% year-over-year decline in total shipments, well ahead of second-place Motorola, which captured 18% of shipments after a 23% drop. Interestingly, Motorola’s share actually increased one percentage point from a year earlier.

Rounding out the top five were Xiaomi, with a 14% share and a whopping 34% decline, Apple, with a 9% share and a 10% decline, and Honor, with an 8% share and a 27% decline.

Despite the decline in overall shipments, Apple’s shipment share increased by 2 percentage points from 7% a year earlier, moving the company from fifth to fourth place in the region.

Other brands collectively accounted for 16% of shipments, down from 19% a year earlier, with their combined shipments falling 37% year over year.

Here’s Counterpoint on Apple’s performance for Q3 in Latin America:

Apple was the most resilient, with the smallest decline among the top five brands (shipments down 10% YoY), and rose one position to No. 4 in the region. Apple absorbed the impact of price increases better than its rivals, helped by strong product availability. Apple launched the iPhone 18 Pro series at the end of the quarter. For the first time, Chile joined Brazil and Mexico in the first launch wave.

As for regional factors that contributed to the decline, Senior Analyst Benjamin Corona noted that Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia faced additional challenges beyond the global memory shortage, ranging from political uncertainty to inflation and tighter household budgets. Smartphone shipments fell 22%, 26%, and 28% in those countries, respectively.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint says it “expects the decline to ease in Q4 2026 as prices stabilize and seasonal demand returns,” adding that “memory-related price pressure should moderate by Q2 2027, but supply constraints will likely continue through the end of 2027.”

#3171. This iPad Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off During Black Friday

If you're shopping for an iPad this holiday season, you might be a bit intimidated by Apple's price tags. The iPad mini starts at $599; the base iPad Air is $749; and the entry-level iPad Pro is a whopping $1,199. Most of Apple's iPad line certainly lives up to its expensive reputation.

That's where the iPad A16 comes in. This is Apple's least expensive tablet, with an MSRP of $449. But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

The iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

The iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Apple says this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee plans to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

#3163. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus.
